transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-07-30
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Morgan Lee (Redwood AE), Diego Marquez (Redwood SE), Anita Patel (Lumina CTO), Jonas Berg (Lead ML Eng), Ravi Iyer (Platform Eng), Selina Cho (PM)

Summary: Quick discovery on Lumina's real-time clinical triage pipeline: high short bursts of token generation when transcripts are expanded, p95 latency targets around 350ms for 1024 tokens, and need to understand tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem). Customer wants a pilot to validate tokens/sec and p95 under burst loads and table stakes security (SOC2, SSO, KMS).

Topics: p95 targets, burst concurrency, streaming vs chunked responses, prefix/KV cache behavior, quantization/FP16 effects, routing/fallbacks, security/compliance needs, pilot scope and timeline

[00:00] Morgan (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for doing this, I know it's a busy week. Quick intros then we'll jump into how you run inference today and what your p95/throughput goals look like.
[00:22] Anita (Lumina): Hi, I'm Anita, CTO. We handle clinical notes ingestion and then expand into structured summaries. Peak traffic is spiky — at discharge windows we see lots of short bursts. We aim for p95 under 350-400ms for responses up to ~1k tokens, ideally.
[00:41] Jonas (Lumina): Yeah and just to add, our baseline is a homegrown on-prem GPU pool with varying quantized models. We're seeing token/sec collapse when concurrency hits 8-10 clients.
[01:05] Diego (Redwood SE): Okay that's useful. Is that 350ms p95 end-to-end or server-side generation only?
[01:11] Anita: Good question. That's server-side generation measured from request to first token plus finish — basically perceived latency in the UI. We tolerate slightly higher for long completions but the interactive bits need to be snappy.
[01:28] Ravi (Platform): Also, we stream tokens into our front-end as they are produced. So we care about initial token time and steady-state tokens/sec.
[01:42] Morgan: Great. High level: Redwood Hosted gives fastest onboarding but shared capacity; Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools with SLA and predictable p95s; Private is VPC/on-prem if data residency or full control is required. Today let's map which one matches your constraints and what tests we'll run.
[02:10] Jonas: For benchmarking, what do you typically test — batch sizes, kv cache, quantization levels?
[02:17] Diego: We usually vary sequence lengths, batch/concurrency, and quantization. Also we look at prefix/KV cache hit rates for repeated context to measure token/sec improvements. For streaming, measuring time-to-first-token and p95 for first 8 tokens is common.
[02:35] Jonas: Our sequences are often 64-128 prefix and then 900-1k generated tokens. We do a lot of few-shot prompts so context matters.
[02:49] Morgan: That affects kernel selection and memory layout. Quick clarification: are you open to 8-bit quantization or do you need fp16/32 for fidelity?
[02:58] Anita: Clinically we need high fidelity on hallucination-sensitive prompts. If quant reduces quality, we can't ship. But if we can show parity on our evals, 8-bit is attractive for cost.
[03:15] Diego: We'll include a qualitative eval set in the pilot — run samples across fp16 and int8 and include rouge/emd-ish metrics and some manual checks.
[03:26] Selina (PM): Timeline: we want a pilot before our Sep release window. Ideally results by mid-August to inform allocation.
[03:36] Morgan: That's doable. Let's talk targets: you said p95 350-400ms for up to 1k tokens — are you fixing concurrency at user-level (like single-user bursts) or system-level concurrent sessions?
[03:50] Ravi: Both. For single-user we often see bursts of 4-6 parallel requests from microservices, and system-level spikes can be up to 200 concurrent inference calls during peaks. We're primarily worried about p95 tail during those 200 concurrent spikes.
[04:08] Diego: So two axes: latency SLOs per request, and aggregate throughput capacity. For Dedicated pilot we can reserve a few 8-GPU nodes to run a 2-hour stress with realistic arrival patterns.
[04:20] Jonas: When you say arrival patterns, can you simulate our JS streaming client that cancels mid-token sometimes? Cancellations hit your KV cache and sometimes leave small leaks in our infra.
[04:34] Diego: Yes we can emulate cancellations and incomplete KV sequences. We also measure cache eviction patterns. FYI our runtime supports prefix caching and token-level streaming; cancellations typically free KV slots but behavior depends on model and quantization.
[04:50] Anita: On security: we need SOC2, SSO via SAML, and KMS integration — secret keys must be in our HSM. Private deployment might be required if that won't work in Hosted.
[05:03] Morgan: Understood. Hosted can integrate with customer-managed KMS via BYOK in some cases; Dedicated and Private give stronger controls (VPC peering, customer-managed KMS/HSM). We'll share the security pack.
[05:15] Selina: Can you also outline price tradeoffs for Dedicated vs Hosted for bursty workloads? If dedicated nodes are idle we worry about paying for reserved capacity.
[05:25] Morgan: Sure — Redwood Optimize suggestions help: we can do autoscaling with burst capacity and granular commit levels. Dedicated can be configured with burst pools and preemptible capacity to lower costs for spiky traffic. We'll send a cost model after we get your token/sec profile.
[05:44] Jonas: Technical deep dive — Diego, what p95s do you typically observe with an Llama-like open model on 8xA100s for 1k token outputs under 50 concurrency?
[05:56] Diego: Ballpark: on well-optimized kernels and fp16 you might see first-token in ~50-90ms and p95 for full 1k completion depends on tokens/sec — often 7-12 tokens/sec steady-state, so a 1k completion could be 80-140 seconds. But interactive applications often stream earlier tokens and you care more about first 8-16 tokens. For p95 under 400ms you typically need much shorter outputs or specialized models with faster decode.
[06:28] Jonas: Hmm our UI expects shorter emitted summaries (first 64-128 tokens) within that p95. So we need to tune for partial responses.
[06:36] Diego: Exactly; we can focus the p95 on initial chunk latency rather than full completion. We'll instrument both time-to-first-token and time-to-64th-token p95s.
[06:50] Ravi: Regarding quantization: do you have in-house kernels for int8? We tried third-party runtimes and saw worse tail behavior.
[06:59] Diego: We select kernels based on architecture and quant level — sometimes int8 reduces memory bandwidth pressure and improves throughput, but tail latency can increase if it triggers slower fallback paths. We'll test both.
[07:13] Morgan: Let's capture explicit success criteria: 1) time-to-first-token p95 < 250ms for 64-token outputs; 2) time-to-64-token p95 < 400ms; 3) system handles 200 concurrent arrival spikes with <2x baseline p95 degradation. Is that accurate?
[07:38] Anita: Yes, those three look right. Also include no-regression on our hallucination tests (specific prompts) across quant variants.
[07:49] Diego: Noted. We'll include the hallucination prompt set in the benchmark.
[07:55] Selina: For pilot scope, what minimal infra do you need us to expose? We prefer VPC peering and our HSM keys not leaving our control.
[08:04] Morgan: For Dedicated we can do VPC peering and customer KMS binding; for Private on-prem we can run the control plane with a local agent and keep keys local. For the initial pilot, VPC peering + BYOK KMS is probably the fastest to provision.
[08:21] Jonas: Any gotchas with streaming and prefetching? When you do continuous batching, does it add jitter?
[08:27] Diego: Continuous batching is tuned to reduce latency by aggregating micro-requests, but under spiky patterns it can add jitter if batching waits for more requests. Our runtime uses adaptive batching policies to respect latency SLOs; we can pin real-time routes to low-latency mode (smaller batch windows) and background routes to high throughput.
[08:48] Morgan: We'll include routing policies in the pilot config so you can route critical calls to low-latency pools and cheaper calls to best-effort.
[08:56] Ravi: For our observability needs, we need token-level traces and cost per route.
[09:02] Morgan: Redwood Console gives token cost breakdown, per-route latency histograms, and tracing hooks you can instrument. We'll share screenshots in the pack.
[09:12] Jonas: For the Dedicated pilot, can we run a side-by-side against our on-prem infra to compare tail behavior?
[09:18] Diego: Yes we can run comparative runs and supply raw logs. Ideally you provide a small sample corpus and arrival profile and we'll replay it across both environments.
[09:27] Anita: How long does it take to spin up Dedicated for a pilot?
[09:31] Morgan: Typically 48-72 hours to provision nodes and VPC peering once contracts and network creds are in place. The actual benchmark run can be scheduled for a 2-4 hour window.
[09:43] Selina: Are there any licensing issues with models? We prefer open models but need Redwood to handle weights.
[09:49] Diego: We host curated open models and can also bring-your-own weights for Dedicated/Private if licensing allows. We'll enumerate model options in the follow-up.
[09:59] Jonas: Can you also test warm vs cold KV cache scenarios? Some of our worst tails happen right after cache expiry.
[10:07] Diego: Yes, we'll include cache-warmup and cold-start phases in the test, and measure p95 differences. We'll also log KV hit rates.
[10:18] Morgan: Quick note — we'll send a benchmark template with required metrics: time-to-first-token, time-to-64, total completion time, tokens/sec, p95/p50/p99, KV cache hit rate, memory pressure, GPU utilization.
[10:35] Anita: Also please annotate which tests involve streaming vs non-streaming output.
[10:40] Diego: Will do.
[10:42] Morgan: Any blockers from compliance side now?
[10:45] Anita: We need proof of SOC2 + SAML integration example, and confirmation BYOK supports our HSM vendor (Thales).
[10:54] Morgan: We'll push the security pack, including SOC2 attestation and KMS/HSM integration docs. If Private is required per your legal, we can add an on-prem package quote.
[11:03] Ravi: One last technical: for routing/fallbacks, if a low-latency pool is saturated, do you automatically fallback to a cheaper model and then stream a partial response? We want graceful degradation not failures.
[11:16] Diego: Yes we support policy-based fallbacks — you can configure degrade-to-smaller-model or region fallback. We can show a demo of canary and auto-fallback during the pilot.
[11:27] Jonas: That sounds good. A follow-up: will you give us the raw token timing logs so we can ingest into our telemetry?
[11:34] Diego: Yep, raw logs and per-token timing traces will be shared. We'll also provide parsing scripts.
[11:41] Morgan: Let's capture next steps — I'll read them out. Diego will run the test plan and Morgan will send the pilot checklist and security pack. Customer to confirm VPC peering windows and HSM vendor by next week.
[11:55] Anita: Sounds good. Quick question — cost model: if we see 200 concurrent spikes but average utilization is low, how do you structure billing?
[12:06] Morgan: We have commit tiers for Dedicated plus burst billing for short durations. We'll craft a model once we get your token/sec distribution. For Hosted, it's pay-as-you-go but less predictable at tail if you need guaranteed p95.
[12:21] Selina: Any sample dashboards you'll share?
[12:24] Diego: Yes, sample Redwood Console dashboards and a benchmark report template.
[12:29] Morgan: Ok let's do a short recap and assign owners.
[12:33] (recap) Morgan: Next steps: Diego run perf tests & share logs; Morgan send pilot checklist, pricing, security pack; Anita confirm HSM/peering windows.
[12:46] Anita: Thanks everyone, we look forward to the pilot.
[12:49] Morgan: Thanks, we'll follow up in email with links.

End of transcript.

Notes: Transcription contains typical ASR noise - some product names may be slightly off (e.g., "Redwood Dedicated" vs "Redwood Dedicated"). There are a few partial overlaps on speaker labels where the meeting capture had brief crosstalk.
